title: Ranjeev Puri Could Become the First Indian American State House Speaker in the US
excerpt: Michigan's House Democratic leader needs a Democratic flip on November 3 and a caucus vote to make history — as both parties court the state's Indian-American voters.
body:
• Michigan House Democratic Leader Ranjeev Puri could become the first Indian American Speaker of a state House in US history — if Democrats flip the Michigan House on November 3 and his caucus elects him.
  • Republicans currently control the Michigan House under Speaker Matt Hall, while Democrats hold the state Senate and the governorship; Puri, of Canton, is on the ballot for re-election in the 24th District.
  • Both parties are openly courting Michigan's Indian-American voters three weeks before the midterms — Republicans promoted community backing for Senate nominee Mike Rogers at an Oakland County event.
  • A review of state legislative records found no Indian American has served as Speaker of a state House or Assembly; the highest so far have been deputy speakers in New Jersey.

Michigan has become an unlikely centre of Indian-American political attention three weeks before the November 3 midterm elections, with both parties courting the community — and Democrats promoting the prospect of a US first: Ranjeev Puri as the first Indian American Speaker of a state House. A Democratic state House campaign posting said Democrats were "about to flip the state house and make Ranjeev Puri the first Indian American State House Speaker in the country," according to IANS reporting.

What has to happen

The path is specific. Puri, a Democrat from Canton in Wayne County, has been House Democratic Leader since January 2025 and represents the 24th District. He becomes Speaker only if two things happen: Democrats win a majority in a chamber Republicans currently control under Speaker Matt Hall, and Puri's caucus then elects him to the post. Democrats already hold Michigan's Senate and governorship, so a House flip would restore a Democratic trifecta in Lansing. After the August 4 primary, Puri said House Democrats' mission was "to take back the Michigan House, restore our Democratic trifecta, and keep our state moving forward."

https://x.com/EconomicTimes/status/2109865473722785866

The other side of the courtship

Republicans are making their own play for the same voters. The Michigan Republican Party posted that "the Indian-American community in Michigan is coming out big-time for Mike Rogers and our entire Republican ticket," billing it as a live update from Oakland County and naming Michigan GOP Co-Chair Sunny Reddy and Republican National Committee National Committeewoman Hima Kolanagireddy, both Indian Americans, among those at the event. The party gave no turnout or support figures for its claim. The two-sided courtship mirrors a national pattern The Videshi has tracked this cycle, including Indian-American Republicans running amid the GOP's H-1B backlash.

A barrier that has held

A review of state legislative leadership records found no Indian American who has served as Speaker of a state House or Assembly. Indian Americans have held senior posts one rung below — Upendra Chivukula and Raj Mukherji both served as deputy speakers of the New Jersey General Assembly. Puri's own career already carries firsts: born in Racine, Wisconsin, to Punjabi immigrant parents, he worked on Barack Obama's presidential campaign, earned an MBA from the University of Chicago's Booth School, and worked in business development at Fiat-Chrysler before winning his seat in 2020 — becoming, as his record notes, the first Sikh American elected to Michigan's legislature and its youngest Asian-American member at the time.

What's next

Everything turns on November 3: Puri's own re-election, the House majority, and then the caucus vote. If all three land, an Indian American will hold a Speaker's gavel for the first time in US state history — in a battleground state both parties now treat as a proving ground for courting Indian-American voters.
